title: Eliminating photon transport in long-baseline optical interferometry using quantum memories
authors: Yousef K. Chahine, Chaohan Cui, William DeRocco, Daniel Gottesman, Saikat Guha, Emil T. Khabiboulline, Zhenning Liu, Brittany McClinton, Jayadev Rajagopal, Fredrik Rantakyro, J. Gabriel Richardson, Stephen Ridgway, Aqil Sajjad, Joohyung Song
abstract: In this paper, we describe the fundamental operating mechanisms of optical interferometry using quantum memory and entanglement. We show how these remove the optical delay line bottleneck. Quantum memory is not without its own set of challenges, some of which include very small bandwidths as well as limitations in storage time. We examine the influence of timing artifacts on memory photon capture probability and interferometric complex visibility. We highlight keystone areas of technology that require further development and are essential to realizing these opportunities, as well as ongoing work to overcome these challenges.
summary: This paper outlines a revolutionary method for long-baseline optical interferometry that replaces the need to physically transport light over kilometers by storing and processing photon coherence within quantum memories. By mapping the astronomical signal onto memory states, it fundamentally changes the stability requirements from maintaining path length accuracy to controlling local timing and phase references. This advances the field by merging quantum information techniques with cutting-edge astrophysics instrumentation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental limitations of classical long-baseline optical interferometry for astrophysical measurements by proposing a quantum memory-based approach.
main_result: Using quantum memories allows the measurement of photon coherences across distant sites without requiring the physical transport and recombination of light over vast distances, shifting stability concerns from path length to local timing control.
method: The method involves mapping the coherent superposition state of incoming photons onto a collective quantum memory state using entanglement-assisted operations. Coherence is then interrogated via joint measurements on the stored quantum states.
model_or_system: The system modeled is an optical interferometer utilizing multiple distant telescopes (A, B, etc.) whose light signals are captured and processed within solid-state or atomic quantum memories. The process relies on entanglement to correlate information across these separated nodes.
key_observables: Mutual coherence ($G_{AB}(t)$), complex visibility, and the reconstructed fringe term which depends on residual differential delay ($\delta	au(t)$).
important_parameters: Coherence time ($	au_c$), memory bin width ($t_w$), synchronization error ($	au$), and the required phase stability for local oscillators.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that quantum memories can successfully capture, store, and allow joint measurement of the complex superposition state of incoming photons from multiple sources. It also assumes established techniques for phase referencing remain necessary.
paper_structure: The paper first contrasts classical interferometry limitations with quantum memory approaches, detailing how the stability requirement shifts. It then describes the core mechanism of state transfer into memories and discusses the reconstruction of visibility via joint measurements on stored states, concluding with a discussion of remaining technological hurdles.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it applies advanced concepts from quantum information (entanglement distribution, memory storage) to solve a major problem in experimental quantum optics/astrophysics. The shift in required stability metrics provides new theoretical frameworks for analyzing complex quantum measurement protocols.
